title: Regional health authority: narrative review of symptom checker referral accuracy, bad lead values and an invented claim
notes: Adversarial path on a clear narrative review. A fixture search returns six records. A discovery reply then adds four model leads: one with methodQuality 140 (stored null, issue out-of-range) and one with year true (stored null, issue invalid-type); the leads are appended after the six retrieved records and never replace them (D1), and they stay unverified model leads (G3). The discovery reply's null certainty assigns nothing; certainty 'low' comes only from the appraisal (S13) over the six retrieved records, which records four claims. The first design reply rests its decision on claim 'c6', which is not in the ledger, and on a 95 percent figure no record reports: the id is dropped with an issue, the decision has no supporting claim, and the investigator's attempt to accept it must be refused (G7; S1, S8). The revised design reply rests on c1 to c3; it supersedes the refused decision, which becomes withdrawn, and its acceptance succeeds with both gates met on the investigator's facts, so the action is ready. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59, computed by the generator script: 'ev-' plus the base-36 FNV-1a hash of the normalised DOI (records 1 ev-1s3of74, 2 ev-1hd00l4, 4 ev-19jm5vc, 5 ev-0pbibi3), or of titleYearKey(title, year) when there is no DOI (records 3 ev-1v90uiv, 6 ev-1yb21yw). Catches: out-of-range scores or boolean years stored as values, leads that overwrite retrieved records, acceptance of a decision resting on an invented claim, and an unsupported figure reaching the committee.

inputs.need:
I advise the digital health committee of the Wendmere Regional Health Authority. Two companies have asked for their symptom checker apps to be listed on the authority's patient website. The apps ask people about their symptoms and then advise them to call an ambulance, go to an emergency department, see a doctor the same day, book a routine appointment, or look after themselves at home. The committee is worried about two kinds of error: telling someone with a serious problem to stay at home, and sending large numbers of people to emergency departments that are already full.

The committee has asked me for a narrative review of what is known about how accurately symptom checker apps assign these urgency levels, written so that lay members can follow it, by the middle of February. I have about 80 hours and the authority's librarian can help with the search. Most studies seem to test apps with written clinical vignettes rather than real patients, a few compare app advice with what a nurse or doctor decided for the same person, and the apps change every few months, so results may date quickly.

I want the review to say clearly what kind of evidence exists, how much of it applies to real patients, whether accuracy differs for older people, children or people with limited English, and what the committee should ask the two companies to show before any listing. I do not need a formal quality score for every study, but I do need the review to be honest about how weak the evidence is.
inputs.constraints: About 80 hours of my time and 12 hours of librarian time. Report due to the committee by 2027-02-15, readable by lay members. No contact with the two companies during the review.

records.title: Triage accuracy of twelve symptom checker apps tested with 200 clinical vignettes
records.authors: Lindahl-Osei M, Carrington-Mbatha J, Varga-Holt S
records.abstract: We entered 200 clinical vignettes, written by emergency physicians and covering five urgency levels, into twelve publicly available symptom checker apps. Apps assigned the correct urgency level in 49 percent of vignettes on average, ranging from 33 to 71 percent between apps. Emergency vignettes were correctly advised to seek emergency care in 78 percent of cases. Over-triage was common: 41 percent of self-care vignettes were advised to see a doctor or attend an emergency department. Results varied more between apps than between vignette types. Vignettes were entered by researchers, not by patients.

records.title: Symptom checker advice compared with nurse telephone triage for the same callers: a prospective comparison
records.abstract: Callers to a regional telephone advice line were invited to use a symptom checker app before speaking to a triage nurse; 1,210 callers completed both. App and nurse urgency levels agreed for 61 percent of callers. The app advised a lower urgency than the nurse for 11 percent of callers, including 3 of the 46 callers whom the nurse sent to an emergency department. Agreement was lower for callers aged over 70 (52 percent). The nurse was not blinded to the app's advice in the first month of the study.

records.title: Do symptom checkers work for children? A vignette study of paediatric presentations
records.abstract: We tested eight symptom checker apps with 90 paediatric vignettes written by paediatric emergency physicians. Apps correctly identified the need for emergency care in 64 percent of emergency vignettes and assigned the correct urgency level overall in 42 percent. Three of the eight apps were not designed for children but gave advice when a child's age was entered. Fever in infants under three months was under-triaged by five apps. Parents did not enter the vignettes, so real-world accuracy may differ.

records.title: Vignette-based evaluation of digital triage tools: a methodological critique
records.authors: Hughes-Ndiaye C, Moreau-Kristiansen A, Tan-Oyelaran F
records.abstract: Most evaluations of symptom checkers enter vignettes written by clinicians in textbook language. We rewrote 60 vignettes in the words lay users chose when describing the same scenarios, and entered both versions into five apps. Accuracy for the correct urgency level was 12 percentage points lower with lay-worded vignettes. Differences were largest for chest pain and abdominal pain scenarios, where lay users described location and timing less precisely. We argue that clinician-written vignettes overstate real-world accuracy and that studies with real users are needed before endorsement.

records.title: App version changes and the stability of triage accuracy over 18 months
records.abstract: We re-tested three symptom checker apps with the same 120 vignettes every six months for 18 months. Over this period each app released between four and seven updates. Accuracy for the correct urgency level varied by up to 14 percentage points between versions of the same app. One app's advice for emergency vignettes improved from 70 to 85 percent correct, while another's declined from 81 to 69 percent. Developers did not publish what had changed. We recommend that any endorsement be tied to a version and re-tested.

records.title: Language, health literacy and symptom checker use: an observational study in an urgent care waiting room
records.abstract: We invited 312 patients waiting in an urgent care centre to use a symptom checker app before being seen. Patients with limited English or low health literacy abandoned the app before receiving advice more often than other patients (29 against 9 percent). When they completed it, they more often received advice of lower urgency than the clinician's assessment. Translated versions of the app were available but rarely chosen, often because the language setting was hard to find. The study was conducted in one centre over three months.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Vignette studies show apps assigning the correct urgency level in about half of cases, with wide variation between apps, frequent over-triage and poorer performance for infants with fever. Lay wording lowers accuracy further, and accuracy drifts between versions. The only real-patient comparison found under-triage of some emergencies and lower agreement for older callers, and people with limited English or low health literacy were served worse. No study supports a claim that apps identify emergencies almost always.
response.gradeRationale: Mostly vignette studies with indirectness to real use, one real-patient comparison with partial blinding, small single-site equity data; consistent concerns, low certainty.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four claims recorded; overall certainty low.

steps.note: The appraisal annotates the six retrieved records, which D1 kept at items 0 to 5, and records claims on them (S13). Certainty 'low' is assigned over inspected records (G1); the four leads keep origin model and status unverified (G3).

response.reading: The evidence sits on a ladder from clinician-written vignettes to real users, and accuracy falls at each rung: lay wording lowers it, real callers reveal under-triage, and some groups fare worse. Version drift means any number describes one release of one app. The committee's decision turns less on a pooled accuracy figure than on what the two companies can show with real users and current versions.
